primary_sources: Photograph of Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin at Yalta, February 1945

stimulus.text: Photograph of the three Allied leaders seated together on the patio of the Livadia Palace at Yalta, Crimea, in February 1945. From left to right: British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, in a heavy overcoat and holding a cigar; President Franklin Roosevelt, in the center, smiling; and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, in a light-colored military tunic. Military advisers stand behind them, and ornate rugs lie under their chairs.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph by a U.S. Army Signal Corps photographer, February 9, 1945, Livadia Palace, Yalta (NARA 111-SC-260486). Public domain as a work of the U.S. federal government. Viewed before use.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded paraphrases, tables, and photographs (see source_note)
stem: Who are the three men seated in the photograph?

options.misconception: Truman became president in April 1945, two months after this photograph was taken.
Attlee became prime minister in July 1945, after Churchill lost the British election.
Eisenhower commanded the invasion of France, but he did not sit with the three leaders at Yalta.

rationales.A: The photograph was taken at Yalta in February 1945, when Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin met; Truman became president only after Roosevelt died in April.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Truman became president in April 1945, two months after this photograph was taken.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Attlee became prime minister in July 1945, after Churchill lost the British election.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Eisenhower commanded the invasion of France, but he did not sit with the three leaders at Yalta.
rationales.general:
1. The photograph shows three leaders seated together at Yalta in February 1945.
2. From left to right they are Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin.
3. Background: Roosevelt died in April 1945, so Truman took his place at the next meeting, Potsdam.
4. The photograph captures the only wartime meeting of these three men.
Remember: match the faces to the date, since the leaders changed within months.
